summary: This RFC reproduces an addendum to the ISO Network Service Definition (ISO 8348) that defines the abstract syntax and meaning of a Network Address, the address used in connection-mode and connectionless network services.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 941 reproduces an ISO addendum that defines what a network-layer address is in the Open Systems Interconnection standards, and how one is written down. The address names the point where the network service is offered to a program, and it is built in two halves: the first says which part of the world's addressing space the address belongs to and who is in charge of it, and the second is the part the local authority hands out.

questions: what is the iso network address format
what are the parts of an nsap address
what is the authority and format identifier
subtitle: How the ISO standard defines a network-layer address so that any computer in the world can be named.

tldr.problem: The word "network address" is used for several different things: the point where a machine joins a particular network, the point where the network service is offered to a user, and the bits that carry an address inside a packet. The OSI standards needed one precise concept and one precise format.
tldr.mechanism: The addendum defines the NSAP address, the address of a Network Service Access Point, and gives it a hierarchy: an Initial Domain Part naming the subdomain and its authority, made of an Authority and Format Identifier and an Initial Domain Identifier, followed by a Domain Specific Part whose syntax the named authority chooses.
tldr.outcome: The document is distributed for information only and does not specify a standard for the ARPA-Internet. It is a retyping of the ISO draft proposed addendum ISO/DP 8348/DAD2, which had passed a letter ballot in ISO by 10 votes to 4 with 3 abstentions and no votes against.

sections.title: What the Addendum Does
sections.content:
This document is distributed as an RFC for information only. It does not specify a standard for the ARPA-Internet. It was prepared by retyping the text of ISO/DP 8348/DAD2 of October 1984, also numbered SC 6/N 3444, which was undergoing voting within ISO as a Draft Proposed Addendum to the Network Service Definition. Although the RFC has been reviewed after typing and is believed to be substantially correct, typographic errors not present in the ISO document may have been overlooked.

The ISO statement on the status of the document gives the history. At its meeting in Zurich on April 2 to 11, 1984, SC 6/WG 2 produced document SC 6/N 3134 and forwarded it for registration and ballot as a first Draft Proposed Addendum to the Network Service Definition. The letter ballot closed on August 20, 1984, with a result of 10-4-0-3, meaning 10 approvals, 4 disapprovals, 3 abstentions and no votes against. A resolution of the SC 6 meeting in Washington in October 1984 instructed the Secretariat to register SC 6/N 3444 as a second Draft Proposed Addendum to ISO 8348 and to circulate it for a two-month letter ballot.

The addendum defines the abstract syntax and semantics of the Network Address, the Network Service Access Point address. That is the address that appears in the primitives of the connection-mode Network Service as the calling address, called address and responding address parameters, and in the primitives of the connectionless-mode Network Service as the source address and destination address parameters. The scope is the definition of the abstract syntax and semantics of the Network Address. The addendum does not specify the way in which the semantics of the NSAP address are encoded in network layer protocols, and its field of application is the same as that of Clause 1 of the Network Service Definition, ISO 8348.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an ISO standard published as an RFC for information, not an Internet protocol. It was typed out from an ISO draft that had just been through a vote in the ISO committee. The job it does is narrow: define what a network-layer address means in the OSI standards, without saying how any particular protocol puts that address on the wire.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Network Address
sections.content:
The addendum starts by separating three things that are all called a network address. A subnetwork address is the information a real subnetwork needs to identify a particular real end system, another real subnetwork or interworking unit attached to it. In the public network environment the subnetwork address is what the public network operates on, and the point it identifies is a point of interconnection between a real end system or interworking unit and a real subnetwork, a DTE/DCE interface in that environment, not an OSI service access point.

An NSAP address is the information the OSI Network Service provider needs to identify a particular Network Service Access Point, the point at which the network service is made available to a network service user. The values of the called address, calling address and responding address parameters in the N-CONNECT primitive, of the responding address parameter in the N-DISCONNECT primitive, and of the source address and destination address parameters in the N-UNIT-DATA primitive are NSAP addresses. Because the network service primitives are conceptual, the Network Service Definition specifies no particular encoding of the NSAP address. In both CCITT and ISO usage the terms Network Address and global network address are synonymous with NSAP address, and the term NSAP address is preferred where the distinction matters, particularly in speech.

Network protocol address information, or NPAI, is the information encoded in a network protocol data unit to carry the semantics of an NSAP address, known in the public data network environment as an address signal or the coding of an address signal. The semantics of the NSAP address are preserved by the NPAI, while the syntax and encoding of the NPAI are defined by network layer protocol standards, which also specify the relationship between the address and the encoding the protocol uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The same phrase was used for three different things, so the addendum gives each its own name. A subnetwork address says where a machine plugs into one particular network. An NSAP address says where the network service is handed to a program. And the bits that carry that address inside a packet are the network protocol address information, whose encoding each network protocol defines for itself.

sections.title: Domains, Authorities and Hierarchy
sections.content:
A domain is a subset of the Open Systems Interconnection environment within which identifiers for entities of the same type are unambiguous. The global network addressing domain is the set of all Network Service Access Point addresses in the OSI environment, and a network addressing subdomain is a set of such addresses that is a subset of it. The uniqueness of identifiers within a domain or subdomain is ensured by an authority associated with that domain, and the term authority does not necessarily refer to an organisation or administration: it is whatever, in an abstract sense, ensures that identifiers in the associated domain are unambiguous.

Domains are characterised by the authority that administers them and by the rules that authority establishes for specifying identifiers and identifying subdomains. The authority responsible for each subdomain determines how identifiers are assigned and interpreted within it, and how any further subdomains are created. The operation of one authority is independent of others on the same level of the hierarchy, subject only to common rules imposed by the parent authority.

An addressing authority shall either allocate complete NSAP addresses, or authorise one or more other authorities to allocate addresses. Each address allocated by an addressing authority shall include a domain identifier which identifies the allocating authority. An address shall not be allocated to identify a domain or NSAP if it has previously been allocated to some other domain or NSAP, unless the authority can ensure that all use of the previous allocation has ceased, and the authority shall ensure that allocations are made in such a way that efficient use is made of the address space.

NSAP addresses are based on the concept of hierarchical addressing domains, so they have a hierarchical structure: each domain may be further partitioned into subdomains. The conceptual structure follows the principle that, at any level of the hierarchy, an initial part of the address unambiguously identifies a subdomain, and the rest is allocated by the management of that subdomain to identify either a lower level subdomain or an NSAP within it. The part of the address that identifies the subdomain depends on the level at which the address is viewed. The addendum notes that this conceptual structure should not be considered as implying any detailed administration of NSAP addresses.

Because any NSAP within the global network addressing domain can be identified, a global Network Address can be defined to unambiguously identify any Network Service Access Point, and the OSI protocols established between correspondent network entities convey the complete information contained in a Network Address. An NSAP address identifies the same NSAP regardless of which user enunciated it, and a user given the address of the provider in an indication primitive may use it again in another instance of communication. Restrictions on communications may be placed on grounds of technical feasibility, security or charging; such considerations are not related to network layer addressing and are not discussed.

Two properties are deliberately absent. Network service users cannot derive routing information from an NSAP address, cannot influence the provider's choice of route by means of the source and destination addresses, and cannot deduce from them the route that was used, although it is recognised that NSAP addresses should be constructed so that routing through interconnected subnetworks is facilitated. And the semantics of the address do not say which kind of network layer service is being offered, point-to-point or multipoint, connection-mode or connectionless-mode, nor anything about quality of service such as throughput or transit delay.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses are handed out in layers. There is one global domain covering every OSI address in the world, and authorities carve it into subdomains, each with its own authority that hands out addresses inside it. An address therefore starts by naming the subdomain and the authority in charge of it. Two things the address deliberately does not do is tell you the route or the type of service, so that the same address works however the network is arranged.

sections.title: The Structure of an NSAP Address
sections.content:
The intent of the document is best served by keeping clear distinctions among three concepts: the abstract semantics of the NSAP address, the abstract syntax used here to define those semantics and used by addressing authorities as a means of allocating and assigning addresses, and the concrete syntax in which the address semantics are encoded as NPAI in network layer protocols.

The NSAP address consists of two basic semantic parts. The first is the Initial Domain Part, the IDP, which is a subdomain identifier: it specifies the subdomain of the global network addressing domain and identifies the authorities responsible for assigning addresses in each of the subdomains created. The second is the Domain Specific Part, the DSP, which is the corresponding subdomain address. A further substructure of the DSP may or may not be defined by the authority identified by the IDP.

The IDP itself has two parts. The Authority and Format Identifier, the AFI, specifies the format of the IDI, the authority responsible for allocating values of the IDI, and the abstract syntax of the DSP. The Initial Domain Identifier, the IDI, specifies the network addressing subdomain from which values of the DSP are allocated, and the authority responsible for allocating values of the DSP from that subdomain. The semantics of the DSP are determined by the authority identified by the IDI.

The abstract syntax of the IDP is decimal digits, and the allocation of the AFI ensures that the first decimal digit of the IDP can never be zero. That gives an escape mechanism for protocols that expect to hold incomplete NSAP addresses in a field that normally carries a complete one. The AFI is an integer with a value between 0 and 99, written as two decimal digits. Values 00 to 09 are reserved and will not be allocated. Values 10 to 35, 52 to 59 and 80 to 99 are reserved for future allocation by joint agreement of ISO and CCITT. Values 36 to 51 are allocated to the IDI formats defined in the addendum. Values 60 to 69 are allocated for assignment to new IDI formats by ISO, and 70 to 79 by CCITT.

The IDI formats are defined one by one. X.121 consists of a sequence of up to 14 digits allocated according to CCITT Recommendation X.121, giving an IDP length of up to 16 digits. ISO DCC is a three-digit Data Country Code, giving an IDP length of 5 digits. F.69 is a telex number of up to 8 digits, giving an IDP length of up to 10 digits. E.163 is a public switched telephone network number of up to 12 digits, giving an IDP length of up to 14 digits. E.164 is an ISDN number of up to 15 digits, giving an IDP length of up to 17 digits. ISO 6523-ICD is a 4-digit International Code Designator, giving an IDP length of 6 digits. For the Local format the IDI is null and the IDP length is 2 digits.

The DSP may be allocated by the responsible authority in one of four syntaxes, depending on the value of the AFI: binary, meaning zero or more binary octets; decimal, meaning zero or more decimal digits; character, meaning graphic characters with no national variant plus the space character from ISO 646; or national character, meaning characters from a character set determined by the allocating authority. The addendum notes that in several of the IDI formats there is no discernible boundary between the IDP digits and the DSP digits when the DSP is in decimal syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Every address has two halves. The first, the Initial Domain Part, says which part of the address space the address is in and who is in charge of it. It starts with two digits that say how to read the rest: which numbering scheme was used, which authority is responsible, and whether the second half is written as digits, as bytes or as text. The second half, the Domain Specific Part, is the address proper, and the authority named in the first half decides how it is written.

sections.title: Writing an Address Down
sections.content:
The addendum does not specify the way in which the semantics of the NSAP address are encoded in network layer protocols by a concrete syntax in NPAI; those encodings are specified in network layer protocol standards. It does, however, identify two alternative concrete syntaxes that protocol standards may refer to. The entire NSAP address may be represented explicitly as a string of decimal digits, the decimal concrete syntax, or as binary octets, the binary concrete syntax.

The binary concrete syntax is generated by using two semi-octets for the two digits of the AFI; padding the IDI with leading zero digits if necessary to obtain the maximum IDI length for that format, and then using a semi-octet for the value of each decimal digit; representing a decimal syntax DSP the same way; representing a binary syntax DSP directly as binary octets; and, for the Local IDI format, converting each ISO 646 character to a number in the range 32 to 127, reducing it by 32 to give a number in the range 0 to 95, and encoding that as a pair of decimal digits. If the DSP syntax is not decimal digits, the semi-octet value 1111 is used as a pad after the final semi-octet so that the address occupies a whole number of octets.

The decimal concrete syntax is generated by writing the two digits of the AFI directly as decimal digits, padding the IDI with leading zero digits to its maximum length and writing it as decimal digits, writing a decimal syntax DSP directly as decimal digits, and converting a binary syntax DSP in pairs of octets: each octet becomes a number in the range 0 to 255, the pair generates six decimal digits of which two may take only the values 0, 1 or 2, and the pair is represented by the sequence of five digits gbcef with the value of g taken from a table. If the original binary field held an odd number of octets, the final octet is converted to a number in the range 0 to 255 and represented as three decimal digits.

The maximum length of the NSAP address for each combination of IDI format and DSP syntax gives a maximum of 20 octets in the binary concrete syntax and 40 digits in the decimal concrete syntax. A network layer protocol capable of conveying a string of variable length with a maximum length of either 20 binary octets or 40 decimal digits is therefore capable of encoding the full semantic content of any Network Address.

Two reference publication formats allow unambiguous representation of NSAP addresses in written and oral communication. The Decimal reference publication form is a string of up to 40 decimal digits, the written inscription of the decimal concrete syntax. The Hexadecimal reference publication format is the symbol solidus followed by a string of up to 40 hexadecimal digits, the written inscription of the binary concrete syntax, using two hexadecimal digits ranging from 00 through FF for each binary octet.
sections.plainLanguage: The document leaves it to each network protocol to decide how the address is put on the wire, but it offers two standard written forms that a protocol can use: a string of decimal digits, up to 40 of them, or a slash followed by hexadecimal digits. An address is never longer than 20 octets when written in binary, so any protocol able to carry that much can carry any valid address.
